title: Burnham's Breakneck First Week: A Northern Office, Tax Cuts, and a Message to the World
summary: Andy Burnham hit the ground sprinting. Since entering 10 Downing Street on Monday, Britain's new prime minister has crisscrossed England and Scotland, spoken with over a dozen world leaders, and unveiled a series of symbolic economic measures: a tax cut on household electricity, a £2 cap on bus fares, and a tax break for pubs. "This is a down payment within the first week that says, 'We get it,'" he declared. Central to Burnham's platform is decentralizing power from London to post-industrial cities and depleted seaside towns. On Friday, he inaugurated "No. 10 North" in Manchester, housed temporarily in a building shared with the cyberintelligence agency GCHQ. Critics dismissed it as a gimmick, but Burnham insisted it will be "the nerve center for a rewired Britain." Writing in The Guardian, he argued that for decades, "decision-making power has remained in London," leaving struggling areas unable to turn things around. Burnham inherits a sluggish economy—averaging less than 1.5% growth since 2009—and frayed public services. He also faces a volatile world with little foreign policy experience. He reassured Ukraine's Zelenskyy of "resolute" support and told Denmark's prime minister that Greenland's future "should only be determined by the people of Greenland and Denmark," a clear rebuke to U.S. President Trump's annexation talk. Meanwhile, Iran accused the UK of "complicity" in American airstrikes and threatened "consequences." Burnham has maintained the policy of allowing U.S. forces to use British bases, while the Ministry of Defense stated the UK stands ready to defend itself. Burnham's first week signals urgency—but the real tests lie ahead.
why_it_matters: Where a country chooses to put its government offices and investment shapes job opportunities, transport and schools for young people. Big foreign policy decisions also affect peace, prices and even future career chances.

background_read: Andy Burnham, the UK’s new prime minister, was previously the mayor of Greater Manchester—a large urban area in north-west England that once thrived on cotton and manufacturing.

For many decades, the UK economy has grown slowly, averaging less than 1.5% per year since the 2008–2009 global financial crisis, which squeezed public services and widened the gap between wealthy London and poorer regions like the north of England.

GCHQ (Government Communications Headquarters) is the UK’s intelligence agency focused on signals and cyber security; sharing a building with it symbolises the government’s desire to plant high-tech authority outside the capital.

The idea of moving government departments out of London is not new—Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland already have their own parliaments with many powers, but English regions have had less say over their own affairs until recently.

perspectives.description: Many northern communities welcome a prime minister who openly champions their towns. Cheap bus fares, electricity tax cuts and a second power base in Manchester could bring long‑neglected areas investment and pride.

Sceptics see No. 10 North as a gimmick that won’t real‑ly shift power if the Treasury and major ministries stay in London. They also worry about a rookie leader handling Iran and Ukraine at the same time.

The UK has tried devolution before—Scotland and Wales have their own governments, yet England’s regions remain highly centralised. Burnham’s move echoes past efforts, but lasting change requires sustained legal and budget changes, not just a temporary office.

If the Manchester office closes after a few months or becomes cosmetic, the big talk will backfire. On the foreign stage, Burnham’s first real crisis could define whether his resolute words turn into effective action or reveal dangerous inexperience.
